name: Loop 4.2 — Shipped
html:
Shared canvases, sub-issues, a faster editor. Plus what's coming next month.
Loop
v4.2.0 · mar 14
What shipped this week
Shared canvases.
Sub-issues. A faster editor.
Three of the most-requested features of the year, plus a quiet rewrite that makes the editor 40% faster on long docs. Here's what's new.
▤
Shared canvases
Whiteboard-style canvases that anyone on your team can edit at the same time. With shapes, sticky notes, and live cursors.
⌥
Sub-issues
Break a big issue into smaller ones. Roll up status, completion, and assignees automatically. Up to 10 levels deep.
⚡
40% faster editor
A new incremental renderer means typing latency is gone, even on docs with 10,000+ blocks. No setting to flip — it just works.
See the full changelog

Also in 4.2
• Markdown paste preserves formatting from Notion, Linear, and GitHub
• New ⌘K command palette with search across canvases and issues
• Improved keyboard navigation in the sidebar (j/k to move, x to archive)
• Custom statuses now support emoji prefixes
• Fix: search no longer hangs on workspaces with 100k+ items
Coming next month
AI summarize, async standups, and a public API.

name: Brief — Issue 42
html:
The unbundling of the design tool. Plus: three reads, one tool, one quote.
Brief.
Issue 42 · March 14, 2026

The essay
The unbundling of the design tool
By Maya Chen · 7 min read
For a decade, the design tool was a monolith. Figma sat at the center: vector editor, prototyping, comments, design systems, dev handoff, all in one canvas. The argument was always the same — collaboration only works when the surface is shared. And it worked. Until the AI moment shifted what "the surface" even means.
What's happening now is not a competitor. It's an unbundling. The "draw a rectangle, add a component" parts are being subsumed into adjacent products: Cursor for UI scaffolds, Granola for meeting-to-mockup, Linear for spec-to-flow. None of them are design tools. All of them are reducing the surface area where a design tool was load-bearing.
The interesting question isn't whether Figma loses. It's what the new shape of the design role is when half the artifacts you used to produce — the wireframe, the spec doc, the handoff file — get generated as a byproduct of someone else's workflow.
Continue reading →

Three worth your time
01 Stripe's quiet shift to becoming an infrastructure company
Stratechery · 12 min
02 Why the post-Substack newsletter is bundled again
Platformer · 8 min
03 The compiler is the new framework
Brian Lovin's blog · 6 min

One tool I'm using
Raycast Notes
I keep trying to replace Apple Notes. Raycast Notes is the first one that's stuck — it lives behind a global shortcut, doesn't ask me to organize anything, and syncs faster than I can context-switch.
raycast.com/notes

"The best way to predict the future is to invent it."
— Alan Kay

Thanks for reading. Forward to a friend who'd like it, or:

name: Pulse — Issue 18
html:
The week in software: Rust in the kernel, the open-source AI scaling laws, and why Postgres won.
Pulse.
issue 018 · mar 14

This week
Three things that changed how I'll write code next month.
Rust shipped into the Linux kernel networking path. The first open-weight model crossed 4o on real evals. And Postgres quietly added a feature that makes half my Redis stack unnecessary.
Read the issue

Three stories
01 · systems
Rust in the Linux kernel networking path
It took five years of patches, three rewrites, and one Linus-approved memory-safety argument. Here's what actually went in, and what comes next.
LWN · 11 min
02 · ai
The first open-weight model that beats GPT-4o on real tasks
Not on benchmarks — on the messy, multi-step agentic evals that actually predict whether it'll work in production. The scaling laws still hold, but the open models caught up faster than anyone expected.
Simon Willison · 8 min
03 · databases
Why Postgres won (and what's next)
Pub/sub, vectors, JSON, time-series. Postgres now does all four well enough that the "polyglot persistence" story most of us were sold a decade ago looks like overkill. A retrospective.
Crunchy Data blog · 14 min

Quick hits
tool
Codename Goose — Block's open-source AI agent for the terminal. MIT licensed.
release
Bun 1.2 — now ships a built-in S3 client, native HTMX support, and 30% faster cold start.
deep dive
How Cursor's index works — the engineering blog finally explained the embedding pipeline.
funny
"My team uses kanban" — a single-page interactive that's gone around every product Slack this week.
// sponsored
Want to stop writing Dockerfiles?
Railway builds, deploys, and observes your code straight from your repo. No YAML. Try it free →

That's it for this week. Forward to a friend who'd like it, or reply with what you're reading — I read everything.
— Alex
